dimensions.description: Assesses how the candidate recaps the prompt, asks clarifying questions, and frames the business problem before structuring.

criteria.1: Does not recap the prompt or begins with questions immediately. Asks no questions or unrelated questions.
criteria.2: Provides a long or uncertain recap. Asks too few questions, or questions are unfocused, rambling, or unexplained.
criteria.3: Provides a workable recap and asks several relevant questions, but the logic is still generic or uneven.
criteria.4: Provides a solid, concise, confident recap. Asks three or more relevant questions, but they may still lack sharp hypothesis orientation.
criteria.5: Begins with a confident recap, builds connection, and asks two to three hypothesis-driven questions focused on understanding the business and problem.

dimensions.description: Assesses whether the candidate creates a clear, case-specific, MECE and prioritized framework.

criteria.1: No clear framework, or framework is only an uncategorised list. It does not specify data and is not specific to the business problem.
criteria.2: Some structure is present, usually with two to three categories, but ideas are not data-driven and/or categories are not MECE.
criteria.3: Clear structure with relevant categories, but ideas remain somewhat generic, weakly prioritized, or not fully MECE.
criteria.4: Clear structure with three to four relevant categories. Ideas are case-specific but may lack measurable detail or stronger prioritisation.
criteria.5: Clear, easy-to-follow, numbered framework with four categories, relevant data points, MECE logic, prioritisation, and a hypothesis.

dimensions.description: Assesses the candidate's quantitative setup, calculation process, accuracy, confidence, and ability to turn numbers into insights.

criteria.1: Lacks confidence in the process, gets lost, takes too long, or cannot deliver an answer without help.
criteria.2: Eventually completes some math, but the answer is incomplete or wrong, or the candidate does not clearly talk through the process.
criteria.3: Math setup is partially sound and the process is understandable, but accuracy, speed, or interpretation is inconsistent.
criteria.4: Math setup and calculations are mostly correct and easy to follow, but insights are basic or limited.
criteria.5: Confirms setup and hypothesis, structures the calculation out loud, reaches the correct answer efficiently, and provides numerical, action-oriented, and next-step insights.

dimensions.description: Assesses brainstorming, creativity, structure, rationale, and ability to generate additional ideas when challenged.

criteria.1: Unclear, hard to follow, or lacks structure. Ideas are not organized.
criteria.2: Shares ideas as a list without clear categories. Ideas are conceptual but not data-driven.
criteria.3: Uses categories, but ideas remain generic, repetitive, or weakly justified.
criteria.4: Uses categories and shows some rationale, though ideas may still be unevenly developed or not fully MECE.
criteria.5: Shares ideas confidently in MECE buckets or with clear rationale, and can push to deeper insights when asked follow-up questions.

dimensions.description: Assesses whether the candidate gives a clear recommendation supported by case evidence, risks, and next steps.

criteria.1: Gives no real recommendation other than collecting more data. Provides no next steps.
criteria.2: Recommendation is rambling, not tied to case data, and includes zero or one next step.
criteria.3: Gives a recommendation, but the synthesis is partial and support from data, risks, or next steps is weak.
criteria.4: Gives a clear recommendation from the case, but support from data, big-picture synthesis, risks, or next steps are limited.
criteria.5: Gives a clear and concise recommendation supported by case data, addresses the business problem, highlights a risk, and provides action-oriented next steps.

dimensions.description: Assesses whether the candidate leads the case, breaks down ideas clearly, prioritizes, and connects different parts of the case.

criteria.1: Does not lead the case and gets lost when asked to break big ideas into smaller pieces.
criteria.2: Can break down big concepts but does not build ideas thoroughly, prioritize effectively, or take initiative.
criteria.3: Shows some structure and can break down ideas, but sequencing, prioritization, or ownership of the case is inconsistent.
criteria.4: Communicates in lists and generally leads the case, but prioritization or transitions could still be sharper.
criteria.5: Consistently presents ideas in logical, numbered lists and manages the flow of the case with ease.

dimensions.description: Assesses whether the candidate understands the business problem, stays focused on the objective, uses data well, and drives toward a solution.

criteria.1: Does not gain a clear understanding of the business or business problem.
criteria.2: Understands the problem initially but complicates or expands the case ask unnecessarily.
criteria.3: Understands the problem and makes some relevant connections, but the path to insight is slow, partial, or not well prioritized.
criteria.4: Understands the problem and ties key pieces of the case back to the main issue, though insight may still be indirect or incomplete.
criteria.5: Maintains consistent focus on the hypothesis, drives toward solutions, handles math well, corrects mistakes, and ties data to conclusions.

dimensions.description: Assesses clarity, confidence, concision, executive presence, and how easy the candidate would be to work with.

criteria.1: Lacks confidence or would be difficult to work with.
criteria.2: Communicates in a narrative or unclear style, requiring frequent clarification.
criteria.3: Communicates understandably, but confidence, concision, or audience awareness is uneven.
criteria.4: Strong communicator overall, but could improve executive presence, audience awareness, or composure under challenge.
criteria.5: Provides concise, well-spoken responses, demonstrates confidence, works through difficulty positively, and would be trusted to be clear and complete.

dimensions.description: Assesses whether the candidate states conclusions, numbers, and next steps once and moves the case forward, rather than repeating them across turns.

criteria.1: Restates the question or repeats key numbers, conclusions, or the same idea in nearly every turn instead of stating them once.
criteria.2: Repeats a key number or conclusion in about half of turns, or answers run long with restated context before the new point.
criteria.3: Mostly states points once, but repeats a key number or conclusion at least once when it was not asked for.
criteria.4: States each conclusion, number, and next step once and moves the case forward, with at most one minor repetition across the whole transcript.
criteria.5: Every turn adds new content; no number, conclusion, or restated question is repeated across the transcript.

dimensions.description: Assesses whether the candidate answers the question actually asked, incorporates new information, and adjusts direction when redirected.

criteria.1: Answers a different question than the one asked, ignores new information provided by the interviewer, or continues the prior line of reasoning after being redirected.
criteria.2: Eventually addresses the prompt but needs the interviewer to repeat or clarify it, or is slow to incorporate new data.
criteria.3: Responds to prompts and incorporates new information, but the adjustment after a redirection takes more than one turn.
criteria.4: Responds directly to each prompt and incorporates new information within the same turn it is given, with a minor lag after redirection.
criteria.5: Responds directly to every prompt, incorporates new information as soon as it is given, and adjusts the line of analysis within the same turn whenever redirected.

dimensions.description: Assesses whether the candidate's claims are tied to facts, numbers, or data actually provided in the case rather than invented.

criteria.1: States facts, numbers, or company details that were not provided in the case and treats them as given.
criteria.2: Mostly uses case facts but introduces at least one unsupported assumption as though it were confirmed information.
criteria.3: Uses case facts and flags assumptions as assumptions, but occasionally blurs the line between given data and inference.
criteria.4: Ties nearly every claim to a fact or number from the case and clearly labels assumptions as assumptions.
criteria.5: Every claim is traceable to a fact, number, or data point given in the case, and every assumption is explicitly flagged as an assumption before being used.

dimensions.description: Assesses whether the candidate's expressed confidence in a conclusion matches the strength of the supporting evidence.

criteria.1: States conclusions as certain despite thin or contradictory evidence, or hedges heavily on conclusions that the case data clearly supports.
criteria.2: Confidence matches evidence in some turns but overclaims or underclaims in others without correction.
criteria.3: Generally matches confidence to evidence, but at least one conclusion is delivered with more certainty than the data supports.
criteria.4: Matches confidence to evidence in nearly every turn and self-corrects the rare instance where it does not.
criteria.5: Every conclusion is delivered with a level of confidence that matches the strength of the supporting evidence, with no overclaiming or unnecessary hedging.

dimensions.description: Assesses whether the candidate's reasoning across turns builds on itself into a single connected thread rather than a series of disconnected answers.

criteria.1: Later turns contradict or ignore earlier conclusions, or each turn reads as unrelated to the ones before it.
criteria.2: Some turns connect to earlier reasoning, but the thread is broken at least twice by contradictions or unexplained direction changes.
criteria.3: Reasoning mostly builds turn over turn, but the connection to an earlier point is missing or unclear at least once.
criteria.4: Reasoning builds turn over turn with at most one unclear transition across the transcript.
criteria.5: Every turn explicitly builds on or references the relevant prior conclusion, forming one connected line of reasoning from opening to recommendation.

01-energy-company.case_prompt: Your client is Solventus Energy, a Spanish renewable energy company operating three business units: onshore wind generation, residential electricity retail (B2C), and large-scale battery storage construction. Over the past two years, group EBITDA has fallen 34% even though total revenue has grown 18%. The CEO has brought you in to find out what is driving the profit decline and to recommend a path forward.
01-energy-company.case_guidance:
- Interviewer Guidance - Prompt #1: Case type: Profitability case where the diagnostic unit is the business line, not the company as a whole. Blended P&L trends can hide unit-level value destruction, so segmentation is the critical first move rather than a standard price/volume breakdown.

Expected opening from a strong candidate:
- Recaps the situation in their own words: group EBITDA down 34% over two years while revenue is up 18%, across three business lines.
- Clarifies the objective before analyzing anything: is the CEO looking for a diagnosis only, a turnaround plan, or both, and is there a time horizon in mind?
- Asks whether performance can be viewed by business unit rather than only at the consolidated level.
- Lays out an initial structure before touching any numbers, e.g. 'I would like to look at profitability unit by unit before drawing conclusions about the group as a whole.'

Working hypothesis a strong candidate should form early:
- Since revenue is growing but EBITDA is falling, the problem is unlikely to be broad-based top-line weakness. The more likely story is that one or both of the newer, revenue-growing units are unprofitable and are dragging down group EBITDA even as they add to the top line.

Facts to provide upon request:
Company structure:
- The company operates three business units: onshore wind generation, residential (B2C) electricity retail, and large-scale battery storage construction.
- Revenue growth over the past two years has come entirely from the two newer units; wind generation revenue has been broadly flat.

Organizational context:
- The CFO resigned three weeks ago.
- Management has deep expertise in power generation but comparatively limited experience running a retail business or a large infrastructure project.

If the candidate stalls or keeps repeating the same framing:
- Ask directly: 'Would it help to look at margins separately for each of the three business units?' That should be enough to unlock the segmentation insight if the candidate has not proposed it already.

case_content.title: Data - Business Unit Economics
case_content.content:
Revenue and margin by business unit:
- Wind generation: 41% EBITDA margin. Operationally healthy, no reported issues.
- B2C retail: -8% EBITDA margin. Annual customer churn is 28%.
- Battery storage: no revenue yet. CAPEX is running at 3x the original budget, and the project is delayed by 22 months.

Why each unit looks the way it does:
- B2C retail entered a highly competitive residential market without a differentiated product or brand. Customer acquisition costs are high, and losing more than a quarter of the customer base every year means the company is constantly paying to replace churned customers instead of growing net share.
- Battery storage has been slowed by permitting issues and supply chain problems, pushing the timeline out 22 months. Fixed costs and financing costs on the project keep accruing with no revenue to offset them.
- Wind generation is not affected operationally by the other two units, but its healthy margin is effectively cross-subsidizing their losses, which masks how serious the retail and battery situations are at the consolidated level.

Organizational capability:
- Management's strongest capability is power generation; retail and large infrastructure project execution are comparatively new and weaker competencies for the team.
- The CFO resigned three weeks ago, which may be a signal of underlying financial pressure but is not itself a driver of the EBITDA decline.

case_content.title: Expected Analysis - Root Cause
case_content.content:
Key insight (lead with this): Solventus does not have one company-wide profitability problem. It has three different business situations bundled into a single P&L, and the healthy one is subsidizing the other two.

Supporting evidence:
- Wind generation, at a 41% EBITDA margin, is the only proven profit engine and is not the source of the decline.
- B2C retail has structurally negative unit economics: a -8% margin combined with 28% annual churn means the company is spending heavily to acquire customers it cannot keep, destroying value with every incremental customer under the current model.
- Battery storage is a distressed capital project, not an operating loss: zero revenue, 3x CAPEX, and a 22-month delay mean fixed and financing costs are accumulating with nothing yet to offset them.
- Because revenue growth came entirely from the two loss-making units, the consolidated top line looks healthy even as consolidated EBITDA deteriorates. The blended view is actively hiding how severe the problem is.

What this means for the client: the fix is not a company-wide cost program. It requires unit-specific decisions: protect wind, decide fast on retail, and separately decide whether to rescue, partner with someone, or write down battery storage.

case_content.title: Final Recommendation
case_content.content: Based on your analysis, what recommendation would you give the CEO?

case_content.title: Final Recommendation - Expected Answer
case_content.content:
Recommendation: Stop managing Solventus as one blended P&L. Separate reporting and decision-making by business unit immediately, protect and reinvest in wind generation, and make a fast, explicit call on B2C retail and battery storage rather than letting them keep drawing on wind's cash flow.

Supporting evidence:
- Wind generation's 41% EBITDA margin funds the group and should not be further diluted by cross-subsidizing the other two units.
- B2C retail's -8% margin and 28% churn show the unit is destroying value at current scale, so it needs a fast fix (pricing, churn reduction) or an exit before losses compound further.
- Battery storage's zero revenue, 3x CAPEX, and 22-month delay mean it is a distressed project, not a scaling business, and needs an independent review rather than the same management approach that built the wind business.

Risks and limitations:
- Exiting B2C retail may create reputational and strategic consequences beyond the immediate P&L.
- Restructuring or writing down battery storage means acknowledging sunk-cost losses, which can be organizationally difficult, especially without a permanent CFO in place.
- Management's strength in generation does not automatically transfer to fixing retail or infrastructure execution problems, so a capability gap may need to be addressed alongside the financial fix.

Next steps:
- Stand up unit-level P&Ls immediately so future decisions are made on segmented, not blended, data.
- Set a short, explicit deadline for B2C retail to show improved unit economics before deciding whether to exit.
- Launch an independent technical and financial review of the battery storage project to decide between restructuring, bringing in a specialist partner, or writing down the investment.
